A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison despite reformatting and added experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments across four benchmark games, including exploitability, head-to-head comparisons, and appendix analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds Liar’s Dice experiments, best-response runtime measurements, and a PSRO sensitivity experiment.

M1.justification: Section 4 adds a Liar’s Dice-specific dynamic-programming procedure for payoff computation, exploiting public actions and independent root chance outcomes. This extends the exploitability engine; the evaluated learning algorithms, architectures, and losses remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds 2D5F Liar’s Dice to the four retained board-game benchmarks. Private random dice and public bidding introduce substantially different information and chance conditions from concealed piece placement. Additional Liar’s Dice configurations also appear in the runtime evaluation.

E2.justification: The seven learning methods remain in the exploitability comparison. However, Figure 3 removes Nash and R-NaD from the reported head-to-head matrices, without relocating those results to an appendix. New Table 2 introduces OpenSpiel as a runtime comparator.

E3.justification: New Table 7 tests PSRO oracle-training episode ranges of [2500,160000] alongside the original [125,8000], and Table 2 adds a timed best-response comparison. The main 50-configuration search, 10-million-step training budget, network architecture, and policy-selection procedure remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a targeted test of whether longer oracle training improves PSRO performance (Table 7) and a computational-efficiency comparison with OpenSpiel (Table 2). Existing implementation checks and entropy analyses are retained, with several analyses extended to Liar’s Dice.

E5.justification: Table 7 newly specifies 10th-, 25th-, 50th-, and 75th-percentile exploitability across 50 PSRO hyperparameter samples. The existing three tuning seeds, ten fresh evaluation seeds, interquartile ranges, and standard-deviation reporting remain unchanged; no increase in seed counts is stated.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive Liar’s Dice results and new runtime and PSRO sensitivity results. Table 2 reports 11 seconds for 2D5F best response versus OpenSpiel running out of memory; Table 7’s wider oracle-training range does not improve the listed quantiles. Retained head-to-head values also change: DH3 MMD versus ESCHER moves from 0.55 to 0.52, without an explained protocol revision.

T1.justification: The formal game and exploitability definitions, MMD update in Equation 1, sequence-form mathematics in Appendix A, and deterministic Dark Hex strategy argument in Appendix B are retained. No new formal derivation or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The claimed software and benchmark contribution expands from exact exploitability computations for four large games to five. The policy-gradient hypothesis and principal conclusion that the evaluated FP-, DO-, and CFR-based approaches fail to outperform generic policy-gradient methods retain their meaning.

C2.justification: Section 6 replaces the detailed description of four homogeneous, chance-free hidden-action board games with a limitation covering five games, four somewhat homogeneous. The explicit list of shared restrictions disappears. Qualifications concerning algorithm variants, tuning choices, training budgets, and lack of universal conclusions remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents the Liar’s Dice computation and specifies the runtime-test machine: an AMD EPYC 7413 processor with 256 GB memory. Appendix G revises R-NaD source attributions and removes the note contrasting its retained 50,000 schedule value with a 20,000 source default. The main implementation descriptions and repository access information remain.

R1.justification: New Tables 4–5 substantially expand the account of prior evaluation practices, mapping numerous methods to exact exploitability versus approximate or head-to-head benchmarks and documenting benchmark sizes. Section 4 also cites Brown et al. (2020) as a precedent for the Liar’s Dice computation. The broader policy-gradient positioning remains consistent.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording edits, condenses the game-formalism list into prose, revises benchmark descriptions, and removes v2’s historical erratum. The main section sequence, policy-gradient narrative, and Appendix A–G organization largely persist.

P2.justification: The conference format substantially changes typography and placement. Figure 1 retains fewer board snapshots beside wrapped text; benchmark plots gain fifth panels; Figure 3 changes from eight-by-eight to six-by-six matrices; Figure 4 adopts a logarithmic iteration axis. Four tables are added, and appendix figures are resized and regrouped.

improvement.justification: The stochastic Liar’s Dice benchmark reduces v2’s acknowledged homogeneity limitation, while runtime measurements and the PSRO sensitivity test strengthen the empirical support. However, v3 removes Nash/R-NaD head-to-head results while retaining references to them and changes some retained scores without explanation. These reporting regressions limit, but do not outweigh, the overall gain.
